title: Australia’s AI music decision opens a new front in the fight over human creativity
excerpt: ARIA stripped AI-generated tracks from Australia's charts, ruling recordings must be "substantially human-made." Craig Anderson of Craigman Digital, who has restored masters for Green Day and RHCP, argues the precedent matters far beyond music.
content_html:
TL;DR

ARIA stripped AI-generated tracks from Australia’s charts after an AI-assisted Madonna cover reached number four. More than a third of new Apple Music uploads are reportedly AI-created. Pew found 52% of Americans are more concerned than excited about AI, rising to 73% among 18-29 year olds. Craig Anderson of Craigman Digital argues the issue goes beyond labelling: music’s value is inseparable from human authorship, and AI’s benefits in one domain cannot automatically settle its costs in another.

Wholly AI-generated songs are no longer accepted in Australia. This August, ABC News reported that the Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) stripped machine-made tracks from its official charts last month, ruling that an AI recording can only appear on the list if it is “substantially human-made.” The rule took effect with the August 31 chart, when an AI-assisted cover of Madonna’s ‘Like a Prayer’ became the most-played song on Australian radio and climbed to number four on the charts. Listeners revolted, and ARIA listened.

This also forced a question that the industry had been able to postpone while generative AI remains a novelty. Who, exactly, gets to count as the artist?

The anxiety behind that question is spreading far beyond music. A June 2026 Pew Research Center survey found that 52% of Americans feel more concerned than excited about AI’s growing role in daily life, while 71% believe AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S. over the next 20 years. With adults aged 18 to 29, that figure rises to 73%. Among creative professionals specifically, a Creative Boom survey of nearly nine hundred workers found only one in ten see AI’s effect on their field as positive. Fear has moved well past factories and call centers into industries built on human feeling itself.

Music now offers a particularly potent battleground because the technology is moving quickly while audiences remain attached to the human provenance of what they hear. More than one-third of new uploads to Apple Music were reported this year to be entirely AI-created, according to figures cited by RTE, while major AI music companies are simultaneously striking licensing deals with established music groups.

Yet music has never been just a product. It has carried grief, courtship, protest, and memory across generations who couldn’t otherwise put those feelings into words. Watching a machine manufacture that experience at scale arrives at the same moment millions of workers are being told their own jobs may not survive the decade. Losing income to automation is one injury. Losing the songs that made sense of that loss to the same technology may be another one entirely.

Craig Anderson has spent twenty-five years on the physical side of that industry, restoring and remastering the analog masters behind catalogs from Green Day, My Chemical Romance, Red Hot Chili Peppers, and Alanis Morissette. As founder of Craigman Digital, a Los Angeles archive and digital encoding house that prepares music and film for release, restoration, and preservation, he has watched technology remake the business more than once.

His concern is less about whether AI has a place in creative industries than about the terms under which that place is being established. The present shift, in his view, moves faster and cuts deeper. “AI companies today are looking at the outcry, and they’re backpedaling quite a bit, and they’re readjusting their message,” he notes, pointing to AI companies’ own advertising, which now opens by acknowledging fears over jobs and children’s attention before pivoting to medical and scientific breakthroughs.

“They try to assure us that everything is going to be great, especially in those sectors, but they don’t really address the level of employment, or the downturn in someone’s education, where they don’t have to think anymore,” Anderson adds.

Public conversation around AI, he acknowledges, has been reduced to a contest between enthusiasm and fear. Anderson sees a more consequential question underneath it. Technology can produce useful outcomes while simultaneously weakening the human systems around it, and one benefit cannot automatically settle that trade-off.

He points to the medical field as an example of where the equation can look radically different. A recent medical procedure he underwent demonstrated to him how technological advances can materially improve treatment, while its cost also illustrated the limits of celebrating innovation without examining who can afford it. “It’s great that we’ve got new procedures and technology that will accelerate healthcare, but the medical costs have jumped fivefold with it. It’s all come down to money,” Anderson notes.

Music, he explains, presents a different kind of problem because its value is inseparable from authorship, performance, and cultural memory. Anderson has watched the industry wrestle with automation for years, yet he believes the current wave raises questions that cannot be resolved simply through labelling. “They’re very concerned about superficial compliance, and maybe with enough push from consumers, it could drive the conversation into much more critical territories,” he observes.

Australia may provide an early indication of what that consumer pressure can accomplish. ARIA’s new rules do not prohibit musicians from using generative AI. They establish a threshold for chart eligibility, allowing AI to function as a supporting tool while requiring the underlying recording to remain substantially human-made.

Anderson expects different markets to respond at different speeds. He points to Australia as a market where consumers appear particularly attentive to what they are buying and listening to, while predicting a slower reaction in the United States. Yet the significance of Australia’s decision lies in the precedent it establishes.

Whether its ruling becomes a template or a footnote depends on how loudly other markets echo it. Anderson expects the pressure to keep building, however unevenly it lands from country to country. He remarks, “As long as we don’t get beaten down and worn out by the fight, there are certainly positive things that can come from it.“
